CHAPTER 3.3 · LEARNING AREA 3 · MARCH

Pyramid and cone

The Great Pyramid of Giza, a church spire, an ice-cream cone, a heap of sand: solids with a point. With Pythagoras’ theorem you find their hidden lengths, calculate surface area and volume and, in the land surveying project, go outside to measure for yourself with a tape measure and an angle measurer.

4 LESSONS2 UNITSPROJECT2 LABS
WHAT YOU WILL LEARN IN THIS CHAPTER
  • calculate the height, slant height and lateral edge of a pyramid with Pythagoras’ theorem
  • find the surface area and volume of pyramids and cones
  • understand the curved surface of a cone as a sector
  • in the land surveying project, measure outside, calculate inside and estimate measurement errors

$\pi \cdot 9 \cdot 4$

A sector has the arc $b = 4$ and the radius $r = 5$. What is its area?

$A = \tfrac12\,b\,r = 10$

How do you calculate the volume of a prism?

Base area times height

CAVALIERI’S PRINCIPLEEqual cross-sections, equal volume
UNIT 13 LESSONS

1Surface area and volume of pyramid and cone

The pyramid fits exactly three times into the prism with the same base and height, the cone three times into the cylinder. A cube can even be cut into three identical pyramids whose apexes all lie in the same corner. That is why every pointed solid has a third of the volume.

For the surface area you need the slanting lengths. They hide in right-angled triangles inside: the height $h$ is perpendicular to the base. In a square pyramid, together with half the base edge it leads to the slant height $h_s$, and with half the diagonal to the lateral edge $s$. In a cone, together with the radius it leads to the slant height $s$.

KEY POINT · PYRAMID AND CONE

Pyramid: $V = \tfrac13\,G\,h$ · $O = G + M$; the lateral surface consists of the triangular faces.

Square pyramid (base edge $a$): $h_s = \sqrt{h^2 + \left(\tfrac{a}{2}\right)^2}$ · $s = \sqrt{h^2 + \tfrac{a^2}{2}}$ · $M = 4 \cdot \tfrac12\,a\,h_s = 2\,a\,h_s$

Cone (radius $r$): $V = \tfrac13 \pi r^2 h$ · $s = \sqrt{r^2 + h^2}$ · $M = \pi r s$ · $O = \pi r^2 + \pi r s$

Why $M = \pi r s$? Unrolled, the curved surface of a cone is a sector with radius $s$ and arc $2\pi r$. Its area is $\tfrac12 \cdot 2\pi r \cdot s = \pi r s$ (chapter 2).

Do not mix them up: $h$ is vertical, $h_s$ lies in the side face, $s$ is the edge. Always: $h < h_s < s$.

INTERACTIVE · HIDDEN TRIANGLES

Choose pyramid or cone and set the dimensions. The orange triangle is right-angled; each time, Pythagoras’ theorem is in it.

EXAMPLE 1 · THE GREAT PYRAMID

The Great Pyramid of Giza was originally about 146 m high, and its square base has an edge length of about 230 m. Calculate the volume and the lateral surface area.

$V = \tfrac13 \cdot 230^2 \cdot 146 \approx 2.57 \cdot 10^6$ m³. $h_s = \sqrt{146^2 + 115^2} \approx 185.9$ m, $M = 2 \cdot 230 \cdot 185.9 \approx 85\,500$ m².

about 2.6 million m³ and 8.5 hectares of side faces

EXAMPLE 2 · THE ICE-CREAM CONE

An ice-cream cone is a cone with $r = 2.5$ cm and $h = 12$ cm. How much wafer do you need, and how much ice cream fits inside?

$s = \sqrt{2.5^2 + 12^2} \approx 12.26$ cm, $M = \pi \cdot 2.5 \cdot 12.26 \approx 96.3$ cm². $V = \tfrac13 \pi \cdot 2.5^2 \cdot 12 = 25\pi$.

96.3 cm² of wafer, 78.5 cm³ of ice cream

EXERCISES

A square pyramid has $a = 6$ cm and $h = 4$ cm. Calculate $h_s$, $M$, $O$ and $V$.

$h_s = \sqrt{16 + 9} = 5$ cm, $M = 2 \cdot 6 \cdot 5 = 60$ cm², $O = 36 + 60 = 96$ cm², $V = \tfrac13 \cdot 36 \cdot 4 = 48$ cm³

A cone has $r = 3$ cm and $h = 4$ cm. Calculate $s$, $M$, $O$ and $V$.

$s = 5$ cm, $M = 15\pi \approx 47.12$ cm², $O = 24\pi \approx 75.40$ cm², $V = 12\pi \approx 37.70$ cm³

A church spire is a square pyramid with a base edge of 6 m and a lateral edge of 10 m. How tall is it, and how much roof area has to be covered?

$h = \sqrt{100 - 18} \approx 9.06$ m. $h_s = \sqrt{100 - 9} \approx 9.54$ m, roof area $M = 2 \cdot 6 \cdot 9.54 \approx 114.5$ m².

The curved surface of a cone with $r = 3$ cm and $s = 5$ cm is unrolled. What is the angle at the centre of the sector?

The arc of the sector is the circumference of the base circle.

$\tfrac{\alpha}{360^\circ} \cdot 2\pi \cdot 5 = 2\pi \cdot 3 \Rightarrow \alpha = 360^\circ \cdot \tfrac35 = 216^\circ$. That is the paper cone from the exploration, with all its dimensions doubled.

A cube with edge $a$ is cut into three pyramids that all have one corner of the cube as their apex and one of the three faces not touching it as their base. Show that this confirms the formula $V = \tfrac13 G h$.

Each pyramid has $G = a^2$ and $h = a$. The three are congruent and fill the cube, so each has $\tfrac13 a^3 = \tfrac13 \cdot a^2 \cdot a = \tfrac13 G h$.

TEST YOURSELF!

Volume of a square pyramid with $a = 6$ cm, $h = 4$ cm?

$\tfrac13 \cdot 36 \cdot 4$

Slant height of a cone with $r = 3$ and $h = 4$?

$\sqrt{9 + 16}$

What fraction of a cylinder with the same radius and height does a cone have?

$\tfrac13$

UNIT 2PROJECT · 1 LESSON AND OUTSIDE

2Land surveying project

Surveyors split every plot of land into triangles. In each triangle they measure two sides and the angle between them; the rest is calculation: $A = \tfrac12\,b\,c\,\sin\alpha$. They find the heights of buildings with a distance and an angle of elevation, the volumes of heaps with the circumference and the slant height.

TASKS FOR THE GROUPS
  1. Height: find the height of the school building, a tree or a mast from the distance, the angle of elevation and your eye level.
  2. Area: split the playground or a meadow into triangles. In each, measure two sides and the included angle and calculate the area.
  3. Volume: find the volume of a heap of sand or gravel as a cone from the circumference at the bottom and the slant height.
  4. Check: every group measures one quantity twice in different ways and compares.

Equipment: tape measure or measuring wheel, angle measurer made from a set square, a straw and a plumb line (exploration in chapter 3.2) or an angle-measuring app, chalk, notepad.

Evaluation: a sketch with all the measurements, the calculation, the result with sensible accuracy and a short discussion of errors. Present it in five minutes.

EXAMPLE 3 · A PLOT OF LAND

A diagonal divides a plot of land into two triangles. Measured: 40 m and 30 m with the angle 80° between them, and 35 m and 45 m with the angle 70°.

$A_1 = \tfrac12 \cdot 40 \cdot 30 \cdot \sin 80^\circ \approx 590.9$ m², $A_2 = \tfrac12 \cdot 35 \cdot 45 \cdot \sin 70^\circ \approx 740.0$ m².

about 1330 m². More digits would not be honest for measurements to the nearest metre.

EXAMPLE 4 · A HEAP OF SAND

A cone-shaped heap of sand has a circumference of 12.6 m at the bottom. From the top to the edge it measures 2.5 m. How much sand is it?

$r = \tfrac{12.6}{2\pi} \approx 2.01$ m, $h = \sqrt{2.5^2 - r^2} \approx 1.49$ m, $V = \tfrac13 \pi r^2 h$.

about 6.3 m³

EXERCISES

For the height of the tree from chapter 3.2 (distance 20 m, 35°, eye level 1.60 m), the angle is only accurate to 1°. Between which values does the height lie?

With 34°: $20\tan 34^\circ + 1.6 \approx 15.1$ m. With 36°: $\approx 16.1$ m. An error of one degree makes about half a metre of difference.

A group measures the circumference of a heap of sand 10 cm too large. How much does the calculated radius change? Why does this matter more for the volume?

The radius changes by $\tfrac{0.1}{2\pi} \approx 1.6$ cm. The volume contains $r^2$: an error of almost 1% in the radius becomes almost 2% in the base area.

Plan how to split your playground into at most four triangles. Which lengths and angles do you have to measure at least? Is there a way of measuring only lengths?

Per triangle two sides and the included angle, shared sides only once. It also works with lengths only: a triangle is fixed by its three sides. You then calculate its area with the formula of Heron of Alexandria or via a height.

REVIEW · DEEPEN · CONNECT

A tent has the shape of a square pyramid with a base edge of 3 m and a height of 2 m. How much material do you need for the four sides?

$h_s = \sqrt{4 + 2.25} = 2.5$ m, $M = 2 \cdot 3 \cdot 2.5 = 15$ m²

Connecting with chapter 3.2: what angle do the side faces of the Great Pyramid make with the ground?

In the triangle made of the height, half the base edge and the slant height: $\tan\alpha = \tfrac{146}{115} \Rightarrow \alpha \approx 51.8^\circ$.

Connecting with chapter 2: a cone and a hemisphere have the same radius $r$, and the cone has the height $h = r$. Compare the volumes.

Cone $\tfrac13 \pi r^3$, hemisphere $\tfrac23 \pi r^3$: the hemisphere has twice the volume.

How tall must a cone with $r = 5$ cm be to hold 1 litre? How tall would a cylinder with the same radius and volume be?

Cone: $\tfrac13 \pi \cdot 25 \cdot h = 1000 \Rightarrow h \approx 38.2$ cm. Cylinder: $h \approx 12.7$ cm, exactly a third.

EXCURSIONHISTORY

How Eratosthenes measured the Earth

The greatest survey of antiquity was achieved around 240 BC by Eratosthenes of Cyrene, head of the library of Alexandria. He knew: in Syene, today’s Aswan, the sun stands exactly overhead at noon on the longest day. On the same day in Alexandria, which he took to lie due north of it, a vertical stick cast a shadow. The angle between the stick and the sunbeam was one fiftieth of a full circle, that is $7.2^\circ$.

Because the sun’s rays arrive parallel, this is also the angle between the two places as seen from the centre of the Earth. So the distance of 5000 stadia is one fiftieth of the Earth’s circumference: $50 \cdot 5000 = 250\,000$ stadia. How long a stadion was is disputed. Depending on the assumption, the result is between about 2% and 15% off today’s value of 40,000 km.

Sources: Cleomedes, Caelestia (On the Circular Motions of the Celestial Bodies), Book I. Edition R. B. Todd, Teubner, Leipzig 1990. In English: A. C. Bowen, R. B. Todd: Cleomedes’ Lectures on Astronomy, Berkeley 2004.

HIDDEN LENGTHS

$h_s = \sqrt{h^2 + \tfrac{a^2}{4}}$ · $s = \sqrt{h^2 + \tfrac{a^2}{2}}$ · cone $s = \sqrt{r^2 + h^2}$

$r = 3$, $h = 4$: $s = 5$

SURFACE AREA

Pyramid $G + 2 a h_s$ · cone $\pi r^2 + \pi r s$

CURVED SURFACE OF A CONE

Sector with radius $s$ and arc $2\pi r$, angle $360^\circ \cdot \tfrac{r}{s}$

$r = 3$, $s = 5$: $216^\circ$

SURVEYING

Split into triangles, $A = \tfrac12 bc\sin\alpha$, round results sensibly.

Plot of land: about 1330 m²
